crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Checking claims against the ledger is the practice of testing a stated emissions or sustainability figure against the underlying records that are supposed to support it. In carbon accounting the ledger is the activity data, meter readings, invoices, fuel logs, supplier reports and calculation workbooks behind a reported number. The work sits inside assurance and internal review, where an analyst reconciles what a company says publicly with what its own books and systems show. It covers both the arithmetic, that the totals add up, and the basis, that the emission factors and boundaries used are the ones claimed.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The ledger itself usually lives in a mix of systems: an ERP or finance platform for spend and invoices, utility and fuel data feeds, a sustainability or ESG reporting tool, and spreadsheets that bridge the gaps. Checking claims means pulling from these sources into one working file, often a spreadsheet or a query against a data warehouse, so that each reported figure can be traced back to a document. Version control matters because the same number can appear in a draft report, a regulatory filing and a voluntary disclosure. Access to the source records, not just the summary, is what makes the check possible.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method is reconciliation: take the reported figure, find the records that should produce it, and compare. Analysts recalculate totals from activity data and emission factors, test a sample of entries back to invoices or meter readings, and look for gaps such as missing months or sites left out of the boundary. Where estimates are used, they check that the estimation method is stated and applied consistently. Differences are logged and either explained or escalated, and the result is a documented trail from claim to source. Sampling and materiality thresholds decide how deep the testing goes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The check supports assurance, whether internal or by an external provider, and it depends on records being complete, dated and attributable to a source. Provenance is the point: a figure without a traceable origin is a claim, not a measurement. Controls cover who can change the ledger, how corrections are approved, and how the reported number is locked before publication.Poor records create both reporting risk and legal risk.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: More of this work is moving from annual manual reconciliation toward continuous checks run against live data, with software flagging mismatches as they appear. AI tools are being applied to read invoices, contracts and supplier reports and to match them to ledger entries, which shifts the analyst from data entry toward judgement about what a difference means. That raises its own questions about how an automated match is evidenced and reviewed. Expect tighter linkage between carbon figures and financial records, and more scrutiny of the trail behind any published claim.
